items.excerpt: Not sure if you noticed, but some of today's most addictive [music] and explosively growing products make you feel seen. Like showing you the exact month you'll meet your soulmate. The psychology that makes your product feel built for your users, even if it isn't. To make it even more tangible, I'm also going to show you three products killing it right now by using this to their advantage. By the way, I'm Tim. I've designed products for over a decade from Spotify to a bunch of multi-million dollar startups. So this is stuff I think about 24/7. items.excerpt: It’s only legal in one market. The life insurance market. That probably sounds ridiculous. After all, insider trading is one of the most serious offences in financial markets. If you buy or sell shares while possessing material information that the rest of the market doesn’t have, you can face enormous fines and years in prison. Why? Markets don’t run on money. They run on information. Prices are simply the market’s opinion of that information. When one participant possesses material information that the other side doesn’t, markets stop rewarding good decisions and start rewarding information asymmetry. Governments don’t simply discourage insider trading. They criminalise it. Because confidence in markets depends on participants competing on reasonably equal information. You still don’t know the winning numbers. But every lottery ticket you buy for the rest of your life comes with information that nobody else has. Should you still pay the same $10 as everyone else? Exactly the sort of people who, not that long ago, might have seen actuarial science as an obvious career. I expected at least one of them to mention becoming an actuary. Not one did. That stayed with me. Around the same time, I read the now famous substack on the quiet decline of Australia’s life actuarial market. It articulated something many of us working in the industry have been feeling for years. The Australian life insurance industry isn’t just changing. I wonder whether it’s also quietly underinvesting in one of its most important long-term assets. Its future capability. An asset you won’t find on the balance sheet I’ve written previously about the idea of an Invisible Balance Sheet . Every company carefully manages the assets it can measure—capital, cash, technology and expenses. But every business also depends on assets that never appear in its financial statements. Trust. Institutional knowledge. Relationships. Culture. Leadership. And perhaps the most important of all... The next generation of talent. The life insurance industry spends a lot of time thinking about capital adequacy. I’m starting to wonder whether we should spend just as much time thinking about capability adequacy . items.title: The Chart That Changed an Industry
items.excerpt: In 2014, ASIC released REP 413, its landmark review of retail life insurance advice. The report would become one of the most influential documents in the history of Australia’s life insurance industry. It triggered industry reviews. It influenced government policy. It shaped public debate. And ultimately it laid the foundations for the Life Insurance Framework (LIF). Nearly a decade later, I have a simple question. Has anyone asked whether it actually worked? How We Got Here To understand whether LIF worked, we first need to acknowledge that it was trying to solve a genuine problem. This wasn’t a case of regulators waking up one morning and deciding to reduce commissions. LIF was the culmination of almost a decade of reform aimed at restoring trust in financial advice. The FOFA Era The Future of Financial Advice (FOFA) reforms fundamentally changed Australia’s approach to financial advice. Following high-profile investment scandals, the focus shifted towards conflicted remuneration. The philosophy was simple: Advice should be driven by client interests, not adviser incentives. Investment commissions were largely removed because policymakers believed embedded remuneration structures created conflicts that distorted advice outcomes. Life insurance, however, was treated differently. There was widespread recognition that life insurance advice wasn’t like investment advice. There was no investment balance from which fees could be deducted. No growing pool of assets to fund advice. The concern was that banning commissions entirely would dramatically reduce access to insurance advice. Life insurance commissions survived FOFA. But only just. REP 413: The Spark In 2014, ASIC released REP 413, reviewing life insurance advice provided between 2006 and 2013. The findings were concerning. ASIC concluded that approximately 37% of advice files reviewed failed to comply with ASIC’s requirements. In 2007, Kodak released what was, without a doubt, their most technically proficient 35mm negative cinema film stock ever created. They called it Kodak Vision 3. This formulation wasn’t just a minor tweak; it was a massive upgrade over their older Vision 2 stock, offering unprecedented dynamic range and incredibly fine grain. For almost two decades, if you wanted to shoot a major Hollywood production on color negative film, Vision 3 wasn't just your best option - it was essentially your only option. When the third season of Euphoria dropped, it brought a completely new visual language - inspired by a classically cinematic look from years gone by. The season was shot entirely on a brand-new, custom-engineered, classically cinematic color negative film stock developed specifically for the show. They’ve named it Verita. To understand why Verita is such a big deal, we first have to understand the perfection it was trying to break away from. items.title: How Cinematographers Choose Their Grip Packages
items.excerpt: This video is sponsored by Squarespace: the all-in-one platform to build your website. From the largest swopping crane movements to the subtlest tracking shot, or even a shot mounted directly onto a vehicle, grips are responsible. Grip gear is the backbone of executing any safe and efficient camera motion or rigging a complex lighting setup. As a cinematographer who has worked on both small content shoots or indie productions, as well as industry sized feature film or series shoots, I’ll take you through a typical grips gear package often selected by DPs for both of these different scales of production. From head and legs, to dollies, gimbals and even grips gear for special occasions, let's get started. The one piece of gear that pretty much any production needs is a tripod. But not all tripods are the same. They come in different shapes and sizes and are mainly selected for the payload they can take. In other words, how big is the camera. For our indie shoot, which I’ve assumed will use something like a Sony FX6 or smaller, there are many different options but the tripod kit I’ve listed is the Cartoni Focus 12 with a payload of 12kg. This kit comes with a 100mm bowl tripod head which can be detached and legs that can adjust the tripod height or spread to get lower. To cover any low angles, where the camera needs to get very low to the ground, I’ve included a hi hat, a miniature tripod base which the 100mm tripod head can fit into. Because industry cinema cameras and lenses are larger and heavier, they need a tripod with a larger payload. The industry standard is the O’Connor 2575 fluid head designed for cameras up to 40.8kg - which supports basically any camera and heavy cinema zoom lens. This industry head is paired with heavy duty aluminium legs, which come in a short size, for a lower height, or tall legs for a higher angle shot.
